web_evidence.title: Excerpt from The Last Precinct by Patricia Cornwell
web_evidence.note: An eleven-page Chapter 1 excerpt, explicitly reprinted with G. P. Putnam’s Sons’ permission, sustains Kay Scarpetta’s participating narration through “I,” “me,” and “my.”

web_evidence.title: Tag Questions in Patricia Cornwell’s Novels Black Notice and The Last Precinct
web_evidence.note: A University of Vaasa thesis based on both complete novels explicitly states that they are told in first person from Virginia Chief Medical Examiner Kay Scarpetta’s point of view.

web_evidence.title: Body Language: Corporeal Semiotics, Literary Resistance
web_evidence.note: This scholarly analysis discusses first-person narration as intensifying Scarpetta’s inner struggles and expressly includes The Last Precinct among the Cornwell novels under discussion.

web_evidence.title: Patricia Cornwell speaks about Predator and answers her critics in London, UK
web_evidence.note: A report of Cornwell’s public remarks says that through completion of The Last Precinct she had written the Scarpetta books in first person, restricting experience to scenes where Scarpetta was present, and changed person afterward.

web_evidence.title: Cornwell Abandons Forensics and Scarpetta in ‘At Risk’
web_evidence.note: The Harvard Crimson identifies Blow Fly, the novel following The Last Precinct, as the point where Cornwell abandoned Scarpetta’s first-person narration for multiple viewpoints.

web_evidence.title: Queen of forensic fiction
web_evidence.note: This retrospective alone says multiple, more omniscient perspectives began with The Last Precinct. Its claim conflicts with the authorized prose, book-specific scholarship, and sources that place the change at Blow Fly.

person_note: The Goodreads passages repeatedly expose Kay Scarpetta as the participating “I” narrator, and the authorized opening independently sustains that voice. Two scholarly sources describe the book as first-person, while a report of Cornwell’s own remarks and a separate review locate her move to third-person multiple viewpoints in the following novel, Blow Fly. The lone Los Angeles Times statement that the shift began with The Last Precinct is inconsistent with the displayed prose and book-specific scholarship and appears to conflate this novel’s shift to present tense with the later shift in person. Gnomic uses of “we” or “you,” and brief references to other characters, are local nondiagnostic material rather than alternate narration. The controlling narration is therefore first-person Scarpetta narration; no meaningful structural uncertainty remains.
